content: Nevus anemicus is a congenital condition that manifests as hypopigmented macules of varying sizes and shapes on the skin. These macules are lighter than the surrounding skin, not due to a loss of pigment, but because of increased sensitivity of the blood vessels in the affected area to the body’s normal vasoconstricting chemicals, such as catecholamines. This heightened sensitivity leads to persistent constriction of the blood vessels, resulting in a permanent blanching of the area. Importantly, this blanching is functional rather than structural in nature, and histological examination of the cutaneous vasculature typically appears normal. However, the blood vessels within the nevus do not respond to vasodilators when injected. Differentiating nevus anemicus from other hypopigmented conditions, such as vitiligo, is crucial. When the affected area is rubbed, the surrounding skin becomes red, but the lesion itself does not change color. Diascopy, a diagnostic technique, can help distinguish nevus anemicus from other hypopigmented lesions. Skin biopsy results are often interpreted as normal, unlike in other conditions. Physiological testing can accentuate the appearance of the nevus compared to normal skin. For instance, stroking normal skin typically elicits an erythematous response, but in nevus anemicus, no red flare is observed. Examination under a Wood lamp can also help differentiate the lesion from vitiligo. Nevus anemicus is present at birth or appears in early childhood and is a benign condition. The patches are usually less than 10 cm in size and may be difficult to detect against the patient’s natural skin tone. However, if the surrounding skin becomes sunburned, the hypopigmented area becomes more prominent. Since the histopathology of nevus anemicus is normal, it is considered a pharmacologic nevus rather than an anatomic one. In most cases, the nevus is located in a covered area of the body and is so subtle in appearance that no treatment is necessary.
